query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys subjected to simultaneous mechanical and corrosive stresses, mechanical sliding induces a dynamic process of severe plastic deformation that refines the near-surface microstructure into an ultra-nanocrystalline (and partially amorphous) layer. This microstructural state promotes the rapid and uniform formation of a dense, chemically stable passive oxide film, thereby synergistically reducing both wear and corrosion rates compared to the baseline state.
generation.material_initial_state: A canonical single-phase HEA (CoCrFeMnNi) and a microalloyed variant (e.g., AlCoCrFeNiMoTi with optimized B addition) that initially possess coarse-grained microstructures.
generation.intervention: Conduct controlled pin-on-disc tribo-corrosion experiments in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution under identical load (around 1 N) and sliding speed (0.1–0.5 m/s) conditions for both alloys. In addition, perform in situ microstructural and chemical characterizations (e.g., using TEM, XPS) during and after testing in the corrosive environment.
generation.conditions: Room temperature tests with sliding distances sufficient to induce surface evolution (several kilometers cumulative distance). Parallel baseline experiments include isolated wear tests (in inert atmosphere) and pure corrosion tests (no mechanical load).
generation.structural_mediator: A dynamically formed ultra-nanocrystalline/amorphous near-surface layer that rapidly passivates to yield a uniform, adherent, and dense oxide film.
generation.mechanism: Sliding-induced plastic deformation triggers an inverse Hall-Petch effect and dynamic amorphization in the near surface. This refined, high-energy microstructure facilitates the accelerated formation of a stable passive film when exposed to the NaCl environment. The protective film minimizes friction and wear by reducing direct metal-to-metal contact and simultaneously acts as a barrier against electrolyte ingress, thereby enhancing corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline CoCrFeMnNi alloy, the microalloyed variant is predicted to exhibit: (a) lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates due to the refined surface structure, and (b) enhanced corrosion resistance evidenced by higher corrosion potentials and lower corrosion current densities. Under combined wear-corrosion conditions, the overall degradation rate will be lower than the arithmetic sum of the isolated wear and corrosion rates. This synergy is expected under moderate loads and corrosive conditions but may diminish at extreme loads or highly aggressive electrolyte concentrations where the passive film might fail.
generation.baseline: Wear-only experiments in inert conditions and corrosion-only experiments (static immersion) serve as baselines to isolate individual mechanisms.
generation.boundary: The synergistic improvement should be observable in moderate corrosive and mechanical stress regimes; however, extreme conditions (e.g., very high mechanical load or extremely aggressive corrosive media) may overwhelm the formation and stability of the protective film.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the stability and formation kinetics of the ultra-nanocrystalline layer and the passive oxide film in an aqueous corrosive environment. Additional in situ characterization during tribo-corrosion is essential to validate the proposed mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ characterization (e.g., transmission electron microscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy) on the wear track during and after the tribo-corrosion tests to directly observe the presence and chemical composition of the ultra-nanocrystalline/amorphous layer and the passive oxide film.
measurements: Grain size distribution and amorphous content in the near-surface region
Chemical composition and uniformity of the passive oxide film
Friction coefficient and wear volume under combined and isolated test conditions
Electrochemical measurements (corrosion potential and current density)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in situ measurements fail to detect the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline/amorphous surface layer or if the passive oxide film is not uniformly present (or chemically stable) under the applied corrosive conditions—and if the combined degradation rate does not show a clear synergistic reduction compared to the sum of the isolated wear and corrosion rates—then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. These phenomena can greatly impact strength and deformation/wear resistance. The Hall-Petch equation, σy=σ0+k⋅d−1/2, is fit to the Luo data only, and agrees reasonably well with the nano-grained estimate from Schuh, et al.. This is well described by a recently proposed predictive model that explains the low shear strength and friction coefficients of bare metals and alloys. This model of grain size-dependent shear strength requires no fitting parameters and is based exclusively on materials properties and physically meaningful input parameters like temperature and shear rate. proposals.material_system: CoCrFeMnNi (a canonical single-phase HEA) vs. a microalloyed variant (e.g., AlCoCrFeNiMoTi with optimized B addition)
proposals.intervention: Perform a controlled tribo-corrosion experiment that subjects both alloys to simultaneous sliding wear in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution using a pin-on-disc setup under identical load and speed conditions.
proposals.conditions: Room temperature tests with a normal load around 1 N, sliding speeds typical for industrial wear (e.g., 0.1–0.5 m/s), and testing durations sufficient to allow surface layer evolution (e.g., cumulative sliding distances of several kilometers). In parallel, run separate pure corrosion (no mechanical load) and pure wear (in inert atmosphere) experiments as baselines.
proposals.structural_mediator: A dynamically formed ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer built from grain refinement and partial amorphization induced by mechanical stress, which then rapidly passivates to form a chemically stable, dense, protective oxide layer.
proposals.mechanism: Under combined mechanical and corrosive stress, plastic deformation in the HEA triggers pronounced grain refinement (inverse Hall-Petch effect) and dynamic amorphization in the near-surface region. This ultra-nanocrystalline layer accelerates the formation of a stable, adherent passive oxide film. The resulting dense film minimizes both abrasive wear (by lowering friction and wear rates) and corrosion attack (by inhibiting electrolyte ingress), thereby synergistically improving overall degradation resistance.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline CoCrFeMnNi alloy, the microalloyed variant should exhibit: (a) a lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rates owing to the refined surface structure and lubrication effect of an FCC-rich phase; (b) enhanced corrosion resistance measured via a higher corrosion potential and lower corrosion current density due to the more uniform and defect-free passive layer. When both mechanisms operate together, the synergistic effect should result in a combined degradation rate that is lower than the sum of the individual wear and corrosion rates observed in isolated tests. This prediction should be most evident under moderate load and corrosive conditions; however, at extreme loads or very aggressive corrosive environments (where the passive layer may break down), the synergistic benefit may diminish.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This hypothesis unifies wear and corrosion resistance under a single mechanistic framework—namely, stress-induced formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline surface that rapidly passivates. It explains how microstructural evolution under mechanical load can directly enhance corrosion resistance (and vice versa), thereby governing simultaneous resistance to both degradation modes. The controlled comparison isolates the effects of induced microstructural refinements on combined wear-corrosion behavior relative to well-characterized baselines.

critiques.addresses_problem: The hypothesis directly addresses the research question by linking the mechanical stimulus (stress-induced grain refinement and dynamic amorphization) to the formation of a protective passive film, thereby unifying the wear and corrosion resistance mechanisms.
critiques.constraints: The direction complies with the explicit constraints by focusing on a canonical HEA (CoCrFeMnNi) and a microalloyed variant under room temperature, moderate load, and specified sliding speeds. It also recommends appropriate baseline tests (pure corrosion and pure wear) to isolate effects.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound in that it builds on established observations of inverse Hall-Petch behavior and dynamic amorphization in HEAs under sliding conditions, which facilitates rapid passive film formation. However, transferring these phenomena from a vacuum or inert environment to a corrosive aqueous environment may introduce additional reactive complexities.
critiques.feasibility: The proposed controlled tribo-corrosion experiment, including pin-on-disc tests under identical conditions with baseline comparisons, is feasible with established techniques and instrumentation.
critiques.evidence: Supporting evidence is provided by PMC7311485, which documents dynamic amorphization and inverse Hall-Petch behavior in similar HEA systems. Additional evidence from studies on passivation and wear (e.g., PMC12654518, PMC7866258) further corroborate the approach.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the mechanism assumes that the stress-induced grain refinement and dynamic amorphization in a mechanical contact environment will accelerate passive film formation in a corrosive medium similarly as observed in inert settings. There is potential uncertainty about whether the aqueous corrosive environment might alter, destabilize, or inhibit the formation of the ultra-nanocrystalline layer and its subsequent passivation.
critiques.fix: Incorporate additional controls or characterization to directly observe the formation and chemistry of the passive layer in the corrosive environment, ensuring the mechanism remains valid under all test conditions.

decision.rationale: Direction A directly links the mechanical process of dynamic grain refinement (and associated amorphization) in high-entropy alloys to the rapid formation of a protective passive oxide film. This single mechanistic hypothesis neatly explains simultaneous resistance to wear and corrosion and includes controlled baseline experiments. The main critique regarding the treatment of the aqueous environment is addressed by adding in situ characterization controls of the passive layer’s formation and chemistry, ensuring that the hypothesized mechanisms are valid under corrosive conditions.
